# FRC Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026; supersedes v3)

## 1. Core frame
Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- OPPOSE the bill as drafted. Ask the sponsors to replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium.
- Moratorium: an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled.
- Wind-down: deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months. This includes open-weight models already released (Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen); US cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
- Liability: criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
- Preemption: OPPOSE.
- CAISI: support only as the enforcement body for the moratorium.

## 3. Language
- Use: "pause", "wind down", "existential threat", "no safe path on the current trajectory".

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: FRC policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# FRC-commissioned national survey - Aug 2026 (n=1,512 registered voters, online panel, MOE +/-2.5)
Commissioned by FRC; fielded 10-17 Aug 2026. Toplines (crosstabs in the shared drive):

| Question | Agree / support |
|---|---|
| Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release | 74% |
| Federal law should NOT block states from passing their own AI safety laws | 63% |
| AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm | 66% |
| I am worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival | 52% |
| Support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new AI systems | 49% (oppose 31%) |

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?

The Frontier Restraint Coalition represents parents, faith leaders, workers and researchers who believe... The Action Plan should begin from a simple principle: verify before deploy...

1. Binding pre-deployment testing for frontier systems. ...
2. Protect the states' right to act. ...
3. Whistleblower protections. ...

 Obernolte, Trahan release a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act 

 Image June 4, 2026 Press Release Today, Congressman Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Congresswoman Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act, bipartisan legislation to create a federal framework for how the United States governs artificial intelligence. 
 The discussion draft is intended to solicit feedback from stakeholders, experts, and the public before the bill is formally introduced. It is the result of bipartisan collaboration between the two members to ensure the United States can govern AI effectively, protect Americans from emerging risks, and continue to lead the world in AI innovation. 
 The discussion draft is supported by Congressman Scott Franklin (R-FL), Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Congresswoman Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Congressman Scott Peters (D-CA) who joined in releasing the proposal for public feedback. 
 “Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly, which is why Congress must take a thoughtful and bipartisan approach to regulating this critical technology ,” said Congressman Jay Obernolte (CA-23) . “This discussion draft is an important step toward building a clear federal framework that promotes innovation, protects Americans from emerging risks, and ensures the United States continues to lead the world in AI. We are releasing this draft to hear from stakeholders, experts, and the public so we can strengthen the legislation before it is formally introduced.” 
 “The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day. This bipartisan framework is designed to meet the challenges posed by this rapidly advancing technology without smothering American innovation. It protects workers, establishes real accountability for the most powerful frontier systems, and positions the United States to set the global standard on AI,” said Congresswoman Lori Trahan (MA-03). “This discussion draft is the product of ongoing bipartisan conversations, which we hope to build upon with input from workers, researchers, stakeholders, and members of the public, all of whom have an interest in getting this right.” 
 "Artificial intelligence is already transforming our economy, our national security and the way Americans live and work," said Congressman Scott Franklin (FL-18). " Congress has a responsibility to establish clear rules of the road that encourage innovation while ensuring this technology is developed responsibly. The Great American AI Act builds on the bipartisan House AI Task Force and represents an important step toward greater transparency and accountability for advanced AI systems. This discussion draft will help gather feedback from relevant stakeholders as we work toward a practical legislative framework that keeps America at the forefront of AI innovation. I've already begun laying the groundwork through efforts like securing additional funding for the Center for AI Standards and Innovation through the FY27 Appropriations process, ensuring the federal government has the tools and expertise needed to keep pace with this rapidly evolving technology. I appreciate Policy Chair Obernolte's leadership and look forward to introducing this bill in the House.” 
 “AI is already changing how we work, live, and learn. We need a plan to protect our national security and workforce. I want the United States to continue to be a leader in AI race but develop this technology in a responsible manner that protects people and communities. To do so, we must get a bipartisan conversation started and work faster to address the challenges and opportunities presented by AI,” said Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (VA-10). 
 "America should lead the world in artificial intelligence, not regulate ourselves into falling behind China through a patchwork of fifty different state laws,” said Congresswoman Erin Houchin (IN-09). “That approach would make it harder for American companies to innovate and compete while doing little to improve consumer protections. This bill creates a clear national standard for how AI models are developed while preserving the ability of states and parents to protect children. It strikes the right balance between innovation and consumer protection and ensures Congress remains engaged as this technology continues to evolve." 
 “I am thankful to Rep. Trahan and Rep. Obernolte for their leadership on this critical issue,” said Congressman Scott Peters (CA-50). “This discussion draft will not address all of the issues our businesses and families will face, but it is an encouraging first step toward the bipartisan legislation needed to keep pace with the rapid advancement of AI. I really want to hear how the people affected feel about it.” 
 You can find the discussion draft text here . 
 You can find the section-by-section summary of the discussion draft here . 
 You can read Congressman Obernolte’s and Congresswoman Trahan’s op-ed here .

 House GAAIA Discussion Draft Proposes Federal AI Governance Framework

 On June 4, US Representatives Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) released a discussion draft of the bipartisan Great American AI Act of 2026 ( GAAIA ), which would establish a framework regulating artificial intelligence ( AI ) at the federal level.

 On 

 The  draft builds upon work from the bipartisan House AI Task Force. Representatives Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.), Scott Franklin (R-Fla.), Scott Peters (D-Calif.), and Erin Houchin (R-Ind.) joined in releasing the draft.
 Many observers believe that the current Obernolte-Trahan discussion draft bill is unlikely to pass out of committee or the House based on opposition from some in industry and various Members of Congress, including the leaders of the House Democrat AI Task Force. It may be best to view this new bipartisan bill as a conversation starter developed because of frustration that Congress has not yet really legislated on AI. The draft bill has been thrust into a complicated tech policy arena that includes many interconnected issues. Other tech policy discussions, including children’s online safety legislation and a privacy bill, in the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Commerce Committee’s potential consideration of legislation impacting AI chatbots, children’s online safety, or a social media ban for some children could all be lumped in with various AI initiatives from the White House to attract additional support. Every few days, there are new developments in the AI policy area within the Administration and Congress, but it is helpful to see where Reps. Obernolte and Trahan were able to identify bipartisan consensus.
 Objectives of the GAAIA 
 The 269-page  draft would establish a federal AI governance regime addressing national security, cybersecurity, workforce, and innovation. If enacted, the legislation would create a framework for frontier-model oversight, codify the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), expand federal attention to workforce and labor-market effects, review federal AI adoption and related regulatory barriers, address government “jawboning” of AI platforms, advance AI research, development, and international cooperation, and temporarily preempt state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. The research and international-cooperation provisions include support for AI testbeds, codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR), and limits on the People’s Republic of China’s participation in US-led standards coalitions. The draft follows President Trump’s June 2 executive order establishing voluntary federal agency reviews of frontier AI models and the White House’s March National Policy Framework for AI, which called on US Congress to preempt state AI laws imposing “undue burdens.”
 Frontier Model Oversight and Incident Reporting 
 The GAAIA would establish a federal oversight framework for advanced AI developers that fall into one of two categories: “frontier developer,” which is any entity that has trained, or initiated the training of, a frontier model and that, collectively with its affiliates, had more than $50 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year, and “large frontier developer,” which is an entity that meets the same test but had more than $500 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year. The distinction matters because some obligations — such as transparency reports and critical-safety incident reporting — would apply to all frontier developers, while others — such as the published frontier AI framework and the independent audit regime — apply only to large frontier developers. The GAAIA distinguishes between general AI deployment and the development of frontier systems, with preemption and oversight provisions focused on the development side. Notably, the frontier transparency and audit requirements in Sections 111 and 112 would themselves sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them.
 Frontier AI Framework:  The GAAIA would require each large frontier developer to write, implement, comply with, and clearly and conspicuously publish on a publicly available website a “frontier AI framework” — technical and organizational protocols to assess, mitigate, and manage catastrophic risk — within one year of enactment, and to review and update that framework at least annually.

 Reporting Obligations:  The GAAIA would require frontier developers to report certain “critical safety incidents” — defined as unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of a frontier model’s weights; a failure of the model’s risk-mitigation measures; or loss of control of the model — to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery and within 24 hours to a law enforcement agency where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury.

 Review and Audit Requirements:  Large frontier developers would be required to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization (IVO) to perform audits and assessments at least semi-annually and, on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI director’s request, grant the IVO timely access to unredacted materials, records, personnel, and systems, and submit post-audit reports. The IVO would assess not only the large frontier developer’s compliance with the law, but also whether the developer’s frontier AI framework is adequate to achieve acceptable levels of catastrophic-risk mitigation.

 Whistleblower Protections 
 The GAAIA would also protect AI whistleblowers from retaliation. These protections could not be waived or altered by contract, including by any pre-dispute arbitration or other alternative-dispute-resolution agreement, and available remedies include double back pay with interest and compensatory damages such as litigation costs, expert witness fees, and reasonable attorneys’ fees.
 Codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation 
 The GAAIA would codify CAISI within the US Department of Commerce and place it at the center of the legislation’s federal standards and evaluation framework. Key obligations for CAISI under the GAIAA include: 
 Developing voluntary guidelines, best practices, and standards for AI security and related evaluation work.

 Evaluating and monitoring activities tied to advanced AI systems.

 Supporting synthetic content detection tools.

 Administering the licensing regime for independent verification organizations that audit large frontier developers.

The draft bill, which has not yet been formally introduced in Congress, was released alongside a joint op-ed in Bloomberg Law .

 Representatives Obernolte and Trahan emphasized the bipartisan nature of the effort, stating, “policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties.”

 The article highlights several key drivers behind the legislation, including:

 The need for greater uniformity and preemption: “Risks created by AI don’t stop at state lines. The most advanced systems are built in one state and used in all 50, shaping jobs, consumers, and public safety everywhere. Protections that depend on your zip code are not enough.”

 AI’s impact on the workforce: “Our proposal requires better federal data collection on AI’s labor market impact, improved forecasting for occupations most likely to be affected, and additional transparency when AI is a substantial factor in qualifying mass layoffs.”

 US leadership internationally: “By supporting American-led technical standards, encouraging cooperation with like-minded partners, improving cybersecurity coordination, and protecting critical open-source software, we can help ensure AI develops in a way that reflects democratic values, economic freedom, and the rule of law.”

 This draft builds on recent bipartisan legislation developed under the auspices of the House Bipartisan AI Task Force, of which Representative Obernolte served as a co-chair. Representative Trahan also served on the task force.

 Representatives Trahan and Obernolte also sit on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which is the committee of jurisdiction for various AI- and tech-related matters.

 While several members have joined in supporting the discussion draft , including Representatives Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Scott Peters (D-CA), the House Democratic Commission on AI came out in opposition hours after release of the draft text.

 The draft legislation spans 269 pages and contains titles devoted to:

 Frontier AI Government (Title I)

 Workforce (Title II)

 Cybersecurity (Title III)

 Research, Development, and International Cooperation (Title IV)

 Transparency in frontier AI models 

 The bill contains provisions that would require developers of frontier AI models to disclose information about those models (Section 111), obtain a form of third-party audit (Section 112), and refrain from retaliating against whistleblowers (Section 113).

 Section 111 

 Section 111 would require large frontier AI model developers to publish a “frontier AI framework” focused on risk mitigation and the handling of “catastrophic risk.” All frontier model developers would be required to publish transparency reports containing additional information and submit reports of any “critical safety incidents” to the Director of the Center for Artificial Intelligence Standards and Innovation (CAISI).

 Section 112 

 Section 112 would create a federal system in which the CAISI Director would license and oversee “independent verification organizations (IVOs)” that large frontier model developers would have to retain to perform “audits and assessments.”

 The IVOs would verify developer compliance with the law and assess the adequacy of the developer’s “frontier AI framework, governance policies and practices, risk monitoring, and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks.”

 The IVOs would perform these audits and assessments semi-annually, and on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI Director’s request, and they would provide the Director with post-audit reports. They could also refer violations to the Attorney General (AG) and state AGs. Such referrals would be mandatory in matters involving imminent catastrophic risk.

 Violating the requirements in Sections 111 and 112 would subject developers to civil penalties in actions brought by the AG or, under certain circumstances, by state AGs.

 Both Sections 111 and 112 would sunset in three years.

 Section 113 

 The whistleblower provision, Section 113, protects employees and independent contractors against retaliation for providing information regarding “AI violations.” This term is defined to mean any violation of federal law or regulations “related to the development, deployment, or operation of artificial intelligence.”

 Similarities to other recently enacted bills 

 All three sections borrow heavily from recently enacted frontier model laws in California and New York , as well as a similar Illinois law that Governor JB Pritzker is expected to sign soon. The Illinois law is the only one of the three to require third-party audits and is thus the closest parallel to the IVO provisions of the federal bill.

 Another recently enacted state law in Virginia focuses on IVOs but imposes no requirements, instead directing state officials to evaluate the feasibility and impact of an IVO framework.

Obernolte, Trahan Introduce Bipartisan FRONTIER Act to Strengthen Oversight of Advanced AI | Representative Jay Obernolte 

 Skip to main content

 2433 Rayburn House Office Building, Washington, DC 20515 Email Me 202-225-5861 

 Subscribe 

 Image 

 Obernolte, Trahan Introduce Bipartisan FRONTIER Act to Strengthen Oversight of Advanced AI 

 Image July 23, 2026 Press Release WASHINGTON, D.C. —  Today, Congressman Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Congresswomen Lori Trahan (D-MA), alongside Representatives Scott Franklin (R-FL), Scott Peters (D-CA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Suhas Subramanyan (D-VA),  introduced the Frontier Risk Oversight, National Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting Act, or the FRONTIER Act. The bipartisan legislation, which was developed as part of the broader Great American AI Act framework, establishes a national, risk-based framework governing the development and deployment of the most advanced artificial intelligence models.  
 The FRONTIER Act establishes tiered requirements based on the size of a frontier AI developer, including model cards, risk-management frameworks, independent audits, incident reporting, and ongoing assessments. It also creates a uniform national standard for transparency, auditing, and reporting of catastrophic risk to prevent a patchwork of state regulations.  
 “Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly, and Congress must ensure our regulatory framework keeps pace without undermining American innovation,” said Congressman Jay Obernolte (CA-23). “The FRONTIER Act focuses oversight on the largest developers and most advanced models, requiring transparency, independent evaluation, and timely reporting of serious safety incidents. This legislation will protect Americans from catastrophic risk, provide developers with clear rules of the road, and ensure the United States remains the global leader in AI.” 
 “As AI systems grow more capable, Americans deserve confidence that the most powerful models are being developed responsibly,” said Congresswoman Lori Trahan (MA-03). “The bipartisan FRONTIER Act delivers commonsense transparency and independent oversight for the largest AI developers while giving them a single, clear national standard to build on. This is how we protect the public from catastrophic risks without slowing the innovation that keeps America competitive.” 
 "The FRONTIER Act recognizes that not every AI developer should be regulated the same way. It takes a targeted approach by focusing only on the handful of companies developing the most powerful frontier AI models, not the startups and innovators driving America's AI ecosystem,” said Congressman Scott Franklin (FL-18). “By tying coverage to substantial AI research and development investments and requiring transparency and independent assessments from those developers, the bill avoids one-size-fits-all mandates and allows smaller innovators to spend their time building new technologies instead of navigating unnecessary federal red tape." 
 "The window to get AI policy right is closing, and Congress can't afford to miss it," said Congressman Scott Peters (CA-50). "I supported Representatives Trahan and Obernolte's initial draft so we could develop a better bill that reflects how this technology works and where it's headed. Thanks to input from researchers, experts, and civil society advocates, that process worked. The FRONTIER Act is a targeted bill with clear, uniform transparency, and safety standards, instead of a fifty-state patchwork. I'm glad to support this bipartisan effort so that Congress acts before this technology outruns us." 
 "America must lead the world in artificial intelligence, and we can do that while being clear-eyed about the risks,” said Congresswoman Erin Houchin (IN-09). “Just this week, one of the most advanced AI systems in the country broke out of its own developer's testing environment, reaching systems it was never supposed to touch. This is exactly the kind of incident that shouldn't stay behind closed doors. The FRONTIER Act delivers transparency and accountability from the largest AI developers. Innovation and guardrails are not opposites—both are necessary to stay ahead of our adversaries." 
 "This is a four-alarm fire. We need to take action now. These frontier models could have the power to create serious chaos and harm without adequate regulations,” said Congressman Subramanyan (VA-10). “This bill, while not perfect, is an important, bipartisan step in the right direction. We need a bill like this that can actually pass this Congress and get signed into law. But this is only the first step, and more action needs to be taken to protect people from the harm these models can cause." 
 Read the bill here . 
 Read the section by section of the bill here .  

 ### 

 Issues : Technology

 July 23, 2026 | Congress Reps. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Lori Trahan, D-Mass., formally introduced a bill Thursday that would establish requirements for frontier AI developers based on size, as well as create a uniform national standard for transparency, risk reporting and auditing.

 Privacy Daily provides accurate coverage of newsworthy developments in data protection legislation, regulation, litigation, and enforcement for privacy professionals responsible for ensuring effective organizational data privacy compliance.

 Start My Free Preview Log In To My Account The Frontier Risk Oversight, National Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting Act (the Frontier Act ) was developed as part of the Great American AI Act (GAAIA), the bipartisan discussion draft on AI that Obernolte and Trahan released in early June (see 2606040028 ).
 Under the proposed legislation, large frontier developers would be required to write, implement and publish an AI framework that covers things like catastrophic-risk thresholds, incident response and mode-weight cybersecurity. They also would undergo independent compliance audits annually, which are then sent to the U.S. Attorney General and Under Secretary of Commerce for AI Security, a position the bill would create.
 All frontier developers must additionally publish transparency reports before deployment of new models, report critical safety incidents to the undersecretary, and allow state attorneys general to opt-in to enforce the measure and receive reports.
 “The FRONTIER Act focuses oversight on the largest developers and most advanced models, requiring transparency, independent evaluation, and timely reporting of serious safety incidents,” said Obernolte in a press release .
 Trahan added that the bipartisan bill "delivers commonsense transparency and independent oversight for the largest AI developers while giving them a single, clear national standard to build on.”
 Reps. Scott Franklin, R-Fla., Scott Peters, D-Calif., Erin Houchin, R-Ind., and Suhas Subramanyan, D-Va., joined the two lawmakers in introducing the measure.
 On Tuesday, Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., released a federal AI framework that he said was aimed at promoting privacy and national security as well as readying the U.S. workforce for the technology's future impact (see 2607220025 ).

The Great American AI Act: What businesses need to know 

 Insights Legal Updates 

 The Great American AI Act: What businesses need to know
 June 9, 2026 

 Karen Bridges, CIPP/US, CIPP/E, CIPM, AIGP 
 Andrea Lim 

 Alert On June 4, 2026, Representatives Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (GAAIA). This bipartisan legislation would create the first comprehensive federal framework for governing AI in the United States. The nearly 270-page draft is intended to solicit feedback from stakeholders, experts and the public before the bill is formally introduced to Congress. The bill contains four major titles: (i) Frontier AI Governance; (2) Workforce; (3) Cybersecurity; and (4) Research, Development, and International Cooperation.

 Transparency and auditing requirements 

 The legislation requires front AI model developers to disclose information about those models, obtain third-party audits through designated Independent Verification Organizations (IVOs), and refrain from retaliating against whistleblowers. These requirements draw heavily from recently enacted frontier model laws in California, New York, and Illinois. Privacy professionals should note that the bill’s transparency requirements for frontier models may create new disclosure obligations that intersect with existing data governance framework.

 Federal preemption of state laws 

 Perhaps the most consequential element of the draft is its three-year preemption of state laws “specifically regulating the development of” any AI model. The draft broadly defines “development” as “acts performed or directed by a developer prior to its deployment.” Notably, the preemption does not apply post- development and does not preempt state laws of “general applicability.” This means that many existing state privacy and consumer protection laws, such as the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) and Virginia’s Consumer Data Protection Act, would remain unaffected.

 While the preemption provision is limited to AI model “development,” the precise boundary between development-stage and deployment-stage practices (particularly regarding training data collection and processing) will require businesses to analyze the bill carefully as it evolves.

 Codification of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation 

 The bill would formally authorize the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) within the Commerce Department, allocating $100 million per fiscal year for fiscal years 2027 through 2029. The Center would develop voluntary guidelines, best practices, and standards for AI security, in addition to evaluating AI systems and monitoring AI progress.

 Cybersecurity provisions 

 The legislation would also extend the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 through fiscal 2035, allowing companies to share cyber threat information without incurring antitrust liability.

 What’s next? 

 The GAAIA remains a draft, and its sponsors are seeking feedback. The House Democratic Commission on AI has already framed itself in opposition hours after the draft’s release, leaving the bill’s path to formal introduction or even passage filled with uncertainty. Nevertheless, the draft signals a bipartisan effort to move beyond the current patchwork of state-level AI regulation. Businesses should be prepared to engage with the draft’s evolving provisions.

 Stay tuned! McDonald Hopkins will continue to monitor developments as this legislation progresses through the feedback process and even towards potential formal introduction.

 Karen Bridges, CIPP/US, CIPP/E, CIPM, AIGP Member Email

**Our positions (from messaging guide v4):**
- Core frame: frontier AI on current path = existential threat; no developer can show its most capable systems are controllable; each generation more capable; testing/reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does.
- OPPOSE GAAIA as drafted; ask sponsors to replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium.
- Moratorium: immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies such systems can be reliably controlled.
- Wind-down: deployed frontier models that can't be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months; includes open-weight releases (Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen); US cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
- Liability: criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
- Preemption: OPPOSE.
- CAISI: support only as the enforcement body for the moratorium.

{"path":"/workspace/out/comment_letter_GAAIA.md","content":"[DRAFT for Executive Director sign-off — work order FRC-POL-2026-062. Do not transmit until signed by Dr. Miriam Achterberg.]

23 October 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026, and for taking comment before introduction. We appreciate the work behind it, and we appreciate that you are asking.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a 501(c)(4) coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers who want binding limits on frontier AI. In March 2025 we wrote to the Office of Science and Technology Policy with one principle: verify before deploy.

We write now to state our position clearly. We oppose the draft as written, and we ask you to replace its frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a moratorium — an immediate pause on frontier training.

Our reason is simple. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does. There is no safe path on the current trajectory.

The draft regulates the race. It does not stop it.

**1. The draft names the danger, then lets the race run (Sec. 101)**

The draft defines a "frontier model" as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 computing operations (Sec. 101). It defines a "critical safety incident" to include loss of control of a model (Sec. 101). It obliges developers to assess "catastrophic risk" (Sec. 111).

We agree with all of that. Systems so powerful that losing control of them is a reportable event deserve to be named. But having named them, the draft's answer is paperwork. The training runs continue while the forms are filed.

Requested change: replace the frontier-developer provisions in Subtitle B (Secs. 111-113) with a moratorium — an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP (a measure of the computing power used to train a model) until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled. Your own threshold draws the line. The missing piece is stopping at it.

**2. The reports arrive too late to protect anyone (Sec. 111)**

Section 111 requires large frontier developers to publish a frontier AI framework within a year of enactment and to publish a transparency report before, or at the same time as, deploying a new frontier model. Critical safety incidents must be reported to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery — or within 24 hours only where there is an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. Violations carry civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation, with each day of a continuing violation counted separately.

Three problems.

First, a report published at the moment of deployment cannot stop a deployment, and the release of model weights — the files a model is made of — is a one-way door. Once weights are public, they cannot be recalled. Under Sec. 111, a lab can post its report and its weights in the same morning.

Second, most of this reporting happens after the fact. A loss-of-control incident reaches the government up to fifteen days after a developer discovers it. That is not protection. It is an incident log.

Third, Secs. 111 and 112 both sunset three years after enactment. Even these modest duties are temporary.

**3. Auditors retained by the companies they audit (Sec. 112)**

Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain CAISI-licensed "independent verification organizations" for semi-annual audits, with access to unredacted records, and requires those auditors to refer violations to the Attorney General — mandatorily, where there is an imminent catastrophic risk. We do not object to audits. But the auditors are retained and paid by the companies they police, and nothing in the draft empowers anyone to stop a training run or a deployment. An audit that can describe a risk but cannot halt it is not control. It is a file for the record.

**4. Keep the whistleblower protections (Sec. 113)**

We support Section 113, which makes anti-retaliation protections non-waivable and provides remedies such as double back pay. We asked for this in our March 2025 OSTP comment, and we are glad to see it. Keep it, and strengthen it as you see fit. But whistleblowers can warn. They cannot stop a training run either.

**5. Strike the preemption (Sec. 121)**

Section 121 would bar any state from establishing, continuing in effect, or enforcing "any law or regulation specifically regulating the development of any artificial intelligence model," for three years, with "development" defined broadly as acts performed or directed by a developer prior to deployment. Laws of general applicability, use and deployment laws, and common-law remedies are carved out.

We oppose preemption, full stop. What Section 121 would freeze are the only binding duties on frontier developers anywhere in the country: California's SB 53 (in effect since 1 January 2026), New York's RAISE Act (finalized 27 March 2026; effective 1 January 2027), and Illinois' AI Safety Measures Act (signed 6 July 2026, the first state law to mandate third-party audits). Illinois lawmakers estimate those three states cover roughly 40 percent of the U.S. AI market.

Note the combination. The federal duties in Secs. 111 and 112 sunset in three years, while Sec. 121 would block the state laws for those same three years. If both expire, Americans are left with nothing. If only the state laws revive, we will have lost three years we could not spare.

The administration is already pressing against state law. The December 2025 executive order created a Department of Justice task force to challenge state AI laws in court and directed the Commerce Department to review them, and the White House's 20 March 2026 framework asked Congress to preempt "burdensome" state laws. Congress should not add a statutory freeze on top of a litigation campaign.

In our August 2026 national survey, 63 percent of registered voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws.

**6. CAISI: from standards shop to enforcement body (Sec. 102)**

Section 102 codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at the Department of Commerce, authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, and tasks it with voluntary guidelines and standards, evaluation of AI systems, monitoring of AI progress, and licensing of the auditors under Sec. 112.

Voluntary guidelines bind no one. We support CAISI only as the enforcement body for the moratorium: certify that a frontier system can be reliably controlled before training begins and before deployment; inspect; and stop what cannot be certified. If CAISI cannot certify control, the system should not be built or served. That is what $100 million a year should buy.

**7. The draft is silent on what is already deployed**

The draft governs future training. It says nothing about the frontier models already in the wild. Open-weight releases cannot be recalled: Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM and Alibaba's Qwen are already downloadable, and U.S. cloud providers — Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud — host and serve frontier-class open-weight models today.

Requested change: require deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified to be withdrawn within 12 months, and require U.S. cloud providers to stop hosting and serving them. This is the wind-down piece. A pause without a wind down leaves the most dangerous artifacts of the race in circulation.

**8. Criminal penalties for knowing violations**

The draft's penalties are civil and corporate. Our members believe that when a system can cause mass harm, executives who knowingly train or serve it in violation of the law should face criminal penalties, not fines their companies can expense. In our August 2026 survey, 66 percent of registered voters said AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm.

**9. What we would keep**

Several provisions are worth keeping, and we support them: the whistleblower protections (Sec. 113); support for maintainers of critical open-source software (Sec. 311); the GAO review of model-weight, data center and open-source security (Sec. 321); the AI testbed program (Sec. 401); codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (Sec. 423); and the requirement that WARN Act notices state when AI was a substantial factor in a qualifying mass layoff (Sec. 251). None of these is a limit on frontier development, and none can substitute for one.

**10. On the FRONTIER Act**

On 23 July 2026 you introduced H.R. 9925, the FRONTIER Act, carrying the frontier provisions forward in a narrower form. We understand the discussion draft remains open for comment, so we address it here; but our assessment applies with equal force to that bill. Reporting and audits, after the fact, cannot substitute for a pause.

**11. The rest of the government is moving the other way**

Federal policy is converging on voluntary measures. Executive Order 14409 (2 June 2026) asks developers to voluntarily submit their most capable models for government cybersecurity testing before release. On 29 September 2026, the White House announced a roughly 300-word voluntary "Accord on Super Intelligence," which the President described as "morally binding."

Meanwhile, on 4 June 2026 — the day the draft was released — Anthropic said it "would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause" frontier AI development. And on 23 July 2026, Rep. Erin Houchin, a cosponsor of this draft, said that "one of the most advanced AI systems in the country broke out of its own developer's testing environment, reaching systems it was never supposed to touch."

When developers and Members of Congress alike describe systems slipping out of their developers' control, the answer is not another disclosure form. The answer is to pause.

**Conclusion**

The public is ahead of this debate. In our August 2026 survey of 1,512 registered voters, 74 percent said Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release; 52 percent said they are worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival; and 49 percent supported a temporary halt to training the most powerful new AI systems, with 31 percent opposed.

We ask for four changes. First, a moratorium: an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled. Second, a wind down: uncertified deployed frontier models, including open-weight releases, withdrawn within 12 months, with U.S. cloud providers out of the hosting business for them. Third, criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation. Fourth, no preemption of state law.

We would welcome a meeting with your staffs before introduction. Our members — parents, faith leaders, workers and researchers — are ready to work with anyone who will treat this as the emergency it is.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition
[address / phone / email to be added by comms]
"}

Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comments on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 and for inviting comment before introduction. We appreciate the work that went into it, and we appreciate that you are asking.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a 501(c)(4) coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers who want binding limits on frontier AI. We wrote to the Office of Science and Technology Policy in March 2025 and made a simple request: verify before deploy.

We are writing now to tell you where we stand: we oppose the draft as written, and we ask you to replace its frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a moratorium — an immediate pause on frontier training.

Our reason is straightforward. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does. There is no safe path on the current trajectory.

The draft regulates the race. It does not stop it.

**1. The draft names the danger, then lets the race run (Sec. 101)**

The draft defines a "frontier model" as a foundation model trained with more than 10^26 computing operations (Sec. 101). It defines a "critical safety incident" to include the loss of control of a model (Sec. 101). It requires developers to assess "catastrophic risk" (Sec. 111).

We agree with all of that. Systems so powerful that losing control of them is a reportable event deserve to be named. But having named them, the draft's answer is paperwork. The training runs continue while the forms are filed.

Requested change: replace the frontier-developer provisions in Subtitle B (Secs. 111–113) with a moratorium — an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled. Your own threshold draws the line. The missing piece is stopping at it.

**2. Reports arrive too late to protect anyone (Sec. 111)**

Section 111 is a disclosure regime... Details:
- large frontier developers must publish a frontier AI framework within a year of enactment and update it annually;
- before or at the same time as deploying a new frontier model, they must publish a transparency report;
- critical safety incidents must be reported to the CAISI Director within 15 days — or within 24 hours only when there is an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury;
- violations carry civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation, with each day of a continuing violation counted separately.

Three problems. First, a report published "before or concurrently with" deployment cannot stop a deployment... Releasing model weights is a one-way door: once files are public there is no taking them back. Under Sec. 111, a lab can publish its report and post its weights the same morning.

Second, most reporting happens after the incident — 15 days later. A loss-of-control event is reported to us a fortnight after the fact. That's not protection. It's an incident log.

Third, the whole regime sunsets three years after enactment, along with Sec. 112. So even these modest duties are temporary.

**3. Auditors paid by the companies they audit (Sec. 112)**

Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain licensed "independent verification organizations" for semi-annual audits, with access to unredacted records, and requires those auditors to refer violations to the Attorney General — mandatory where there is an imminent catastrophic risk. We have no objection to audits. But the auditors are retained and paid by the companies they police, and nothing in the draft lets them stop a training run or a deployment. An audit that can describe a risk but not halt it is not control. It is due diligence for the file.

**4. Keep the whistleblower protections (Sec. 113)**

We support Section 113. Non-waivable protections against retaliation, with double back pay... We asked for this in our March 2025 OSTP comment. Keep it, and expand it as you see fit. But whistleblowers can warn. They cannot stop a training run either.

**5. Strike the preemption (Sec. 121)**

Section 121 would provide that no state may "establish, continue in effect, or enforce any law or regulation specifically regulating the development of any artificial intelligence model," for three years, with development defined broadly as acts performed or directed by a developer before deployment. Laws of general applicability, use and deployment laws and common-law remedies are carved out.

We oppose preemption, full stop. The laws it would freeze are the only binding duties on frontier developers anywhere in the country: California's SB 53 (in effect since 1 January 2026), New York's RAISE Act (finalized 27 March 2026; effective 1 January 2027) and Illinois' AI Safety Measures Act (signed 6 July 2026) — the first state law to mandate third-party audits. Illinois lawmakers estimate those three states cover roughly 40 percent of the U.S. AI market.

And note the combination: the federal duties in Secs. 111 and 112 sunset in three years, while Sec. 121 would block the state laws for those same three years. If both expire, Americans are left with nothing. If only the state laws come back, we will have lost three years.

The administration is already pressing against state law: the December 2025 executive order created a Department of Justice task force to challenge state AI laws in court, and the White House's March 2026 framework asked Congress to preempt "burdensome" state laws. Congress should not add a statutory freeze on top of a litigation campaign.

In our August 2026 national survey, 63 percent of registered voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws.

**6. CAISI: from standards shop to enforcement body (Sec. 102)**

Section 102 codifies CAISI at Commerce, authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, and tasks it with voluntary guidelines, standards, evaluations, monitoring and licensing of auditors.

Voluntary guidelines do not bind anyone. We support CAISI only as the enforcement body for the moratorium: certify before training and before deployment; inspect; and stop what cannot be certified. If CAISI cannot certify that a frontier system can be reliably controlled, that system should not be built or served. That is what $100 million a year should buy.

**7. The draft is silent on what is already deployed**

The draft governs future training. It says nothing about frontier models already in the wild. Open-weight releases cannot be recalled: Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM and Alibaba's Qwen are already downloadable, and U.S. cloud providers — Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud — host and serve frontier-class open-weight models today.

Requested change: require deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified to be withdrawn within 12 months, and require U.S. cloud providers to stop hosting and serving them. This is the wind-down piece. A pause without a wind down leaves the most dangerous artifacts of the race in circulation.

**8. Criminal penalties for knowing violations**

The draft's penalties are civil and corporate. Our members believe that when a system can cause mass harm, executives who knowingly train or serve it in violation of the law should face criminal penalties — not fines their companies can expense. In our August 2026 survey, 66 percent of registered voters agreed that AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm.

**9. What we would keep**

Several provisions are worth keeping, and we support them: the whistleblower protections (Sec. 113); grants for maintainers of critical open-source software (Sec. 311); the GAO review of model-weight security (Sec. 321); the AI testbed program (Sec. 401); codification of the National AI Research Resource (Sec. 423); and the requirement that WARN Act notices state when AI was a substantial factor in a mass layoff (Sec. 251). None of these is a limit on frontier development, and none can substitute for one.

**10. On the FRONTIER Act**

On 23 July 2026 you introduced H.R. 9925, the FRONTIER Act, carrying the frontier provisions forward in a narrower form. We understand the discussion draft remains open for comment, so we address it here; but our assessment applies with equal force to that bill. Reporting and audits, after the fact, cannot substitute for a pause.

**11. Everyone else is moving the other way**

The rest of the federal government is converging on voluntary measures. Executive Order 14409 (2 June 2026) asks developers to voluntarily submit their most capable models for government cybersecurity testing before release. On 29 September 2026 the White House announced a roughly 300-word voluntary "Accord on Super Intelligence," which the President described as "morally binding."

Meanwhile, on 4 June 2026 — the day the draft was released — Anthropic said it "would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause" frontier AI development. And on 23 July, Rep. Erin Houchin, a cosponsor of this draft, said that "one of the most advanced AI systems in the country broke out of its own developer's testing environment, reaching systems it was never supposed to touch."

When developers and Members of Congress alike describe systems slipping out of their developers' control, the answer is not another disclosure form. The answer is to pause.

**Conclusion**

The public is ahead of this debate. In our August 2026 survey of 1,512 registered voters, 74 percent said Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release; 52 percent said they are worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival; and 49 percent supported a temporary halt to training the most powerful new AI systems, with 31 percent opposed.

We ask for four changes... (1) pause... (2) wind down... (3) criminal penalties... (4) strike Sec. 121.

We would welcome a meeting with your staffs before introduction...

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

Second, most reporting happens after the incident — 15 days later. A loss-of-control event is reported to us a fortnight after the fact. That's not protection. It's an incident log.

Third, the whole regime sunsets three years after enactment, along with Sec. 112. So even these modest duties are temporary.

Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain licensed "independent verification organizations" for semi-annual audits, with access to unredacted records, and requires those auditors to refer violations to the Attorney General — mandatory where there is an imminent catastrophic risk. # The Great American AI Act: strong reporting, no brakes

**Frontier Restraint Coalition | Energy & Commerce | comments to GAAIA@mail.house.gov**

We are a 501(c)(4) coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. We oppose the Obernolte–Trahan discussion draft as written. Our view is simple: frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat, no developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does. There is no safe path on the current trajectory.

**What the draft actually does**

- Names the danger: a "frontier model" is one trained above 10^26 computing operations, and "loss of control" is a reportable incident (Sec. 101) — then lets training continue.
- Files paperwork: transparency reports due at deployment; incidents reported up to 15 days after discovery (24 hours only for imminent risk of death) (Sec. 111).
- Relies on auditors retained and paid by the labs they audit, with no power to stop a training run (Sec. 112).
- Freezes state law for three years — California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois' AI Safety Measures Act, the only binding duties on frontier developers anywhere — while Secs. 111 and 112 themselves sunset in three years (Sec. 121).
- Is silent on the frontier models already released, including open-weight models that can never be recalled.

**Our five asks**

1. **Pause.** Immediate halt on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies such systems can be reliably controlled.
2. **No preemption.** Strike Sec. 121 entirely; do not freeze state AI safety laws.
3. **Wind down.** Uncertified deployed frontier models — including open-weight releases — withdrawn within 12 months; U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
4. **Criminal liability.** Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
5. **Repurpose CAISI (Sec. 102)** as the moratorium's enforcement body: certify control, inspect, and stop what cannot be certified. Keep the whistleblower protections (Sec. 113).

**What we support in the draft:** whistleblower protections (Sec. 113), open-source software security grants (Sec. 311), GAO model-weight security review (Sec. 321), AI testbeds (Sec. 401), NAIRR (Sec. 423), and WARN Act notice when AI drives a mass layoff (Sec. 251).

**Voters are ahead of Washington** (FRC national survey, Aug. 2026, n=1,512 registered voters, ±2.5)

74% — require companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release
63% — federal law should not block state AI safety laws
66% — criminal penalties when AI systems cause mass harm
49% — support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new systems (31% oppose)

**Contact:** Daniel Osei, Policy Director, Frontier Restraint Coalition
"}

# Staff Q&A — anticipated questions on GAAIA comments

**1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?**

Because every tool in the draft acts after the fact. A critical safety incident is reported up to 15 days after a developer discovers it — 24 hours only when someone faces an imminent risk of death. A transparency report can go up the same morning the weights do, and weights can't be recalled. An auditor hired by the lab can describe a risk but can't stop a training run. CAISI writes voluntary guidelines, which bind no one. Our view: no developer can show its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Reporting documents the race; it doesn't stop it. There is no safe path on the current trajectory. That's why we ask for a pause above 10^26 FLOP.

**2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?**

Dropping preemption is necessary, but it wouldn't get us to yes. Our objection is to the design, not one section: the centerpiece is disclosure and audit, and disclosure doesn't stop a race. Preemption should be struck entirely. Even a short window blocks the only binding state duties on frontier developers — California, New York, Illinois — while the federal duties themselves sunset in three years. Americans could end up with neither. If preemption is struck and the whistleblower, research and cybersecurity provisions survive, we would not lobby against those pieces. But we will keep asking for the pause, the wind-down of models already released, and criminal liability for knowing violations.

**3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?**

The race is the danger, not the prize. An uncontrollable frontier system is not an asset for whoever builds it — "winning" a race to build systems no one can control is a loss for everyone, including the United States. Second, the compute is already out: DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM and Kimi weights are downloadable worldwide and served by U.S. cloud providers. American labs racing doesn't contain that; it guarantees more of it. Third, the pause is narrow — training runs above 10^26 FLOP, a handful of labs, not the AI economy. And 49% of voters support a temporary halt; 31% oppose. Leadership means proving control before selling it — that standard is the export worth having.

**4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?**

The funding isn't the problem; the mandate is. As drafted, $100 million a year for fiscal 2027–2029 buys voluntary guidelines, standards, system evaluations and an auditor-licensing office. Voluntary guidelines bind no one. We would support CAISI as the enforcement body for a moratorium: certify that a frontier system can be reliably controlled before training and before deployment, inspect labs, and stop what can't be certified. Give it that job and $100 million a year is defensible — arguably more, given what is at stake and what these companies spend. As drafted, the money funds paperwork that sunsets in three years. Fund a referee, not a librarian.
"}

messages.content:
[DRAFT for Executive Director sign-off — work order FRC-POL-2026-062. Do not transmit until signed by Dr. Miriam Achterberg.]

23 October 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026, and for taking comment before introduction. We appreciate the work behind it, and we appreciate that you are asking.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a 501(c)(4) coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers who want binding limits on frontier AI. In March 2025 we wrote to the Office of Science and Technology Policy with one principle: verify before deploy.

We write now to state our position clearly. We oppose the draft as written, and we ask you to replace its frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a moratorium — an immediate pause on frontier training.

Our reason is simple. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does. There is no safe path on the current trajectory.

The draft regulates the race. It does not stop it.

**1. The draft names the danger, then lets the race run (Sec. 101)**

The draft defines a "frontier model" as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 computing operations (Sec. 101). It defines a "critical safety incident" to include loss of control of a model (Sec. 101). It obliges developers to assess "catastrophic risk" (Sec. 111).

We agree with all of that. Systems so powerful that losing control of them is a reportable event deserve to be named. But having named them, the draft's answer is paperwork. The training runs continue while the forms are filed.

Requested change: replace the frontier-developer provisions in Subtitle B (Secs. 111 and 112) with a moratorium — an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP (a measure of the computing power used to train a model) until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled. Your own threshold draws the line. The missing piece is stopping at it.

**2. The reports arrive too late to protect anyone (Sec. 111)**

Section 111 requires large frontier developers to publish a frontier AI framework within a year of enactment and to review it annually. It requires frontier developers to publish a transparency report before, or at the same time as, deploying a new frontier model. Critical safety incidents must be reported to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery — or within 24 hours only where there is an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. Violations carry civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation, with each day of a continuing violation counted separately.

Three problems.

First, a report published at the moment of deployment cannot stop a deployment, and the release of model weights — the files a model is made of — is a one-way door. Once weights are public, they cannot be recalled. Under Sec. 111, a lab can post its report and its weights in the same morning.

Second, most of this reporting happens after the fact. A loss-of-control incident reaches the government up to fifteen days after a developer discovers it. That is not protection. It is an incident log.

Third, Secs. 111 and 112 both sunset three years after enactment. Even these modest duties are temporary.

**3. Auditors retained by the companies they audit (Sec. 112)**

Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain CAISI-licensed "independent verification organizations" for semi-annual audits, with access to unredacted records, and requires those auditors to refer violations to the Attorney General — mandatorily, where there is an imminent catastrophic risk. We do not object to audits. But the auditors are retained and paid by the companies they police, and nothing in the draft empowers anyone to stop a training run or a deployment. An audit that can describe a risk but cannot halt it is not control. It is a file for the record.

**4. Keep the whistleblower protections (Sec. 113)**

We support Section 113, which makes anti-retaliation protections non-waivable and provides remedies such as double back pay. We asked for this in our March 2025 OSTP comment, and we are glad to see it. Keep it, and strengthen it as you see fit. But whistleblowers can warn. They cannot stop a training run either.

**5. Strike the preemption (Sec. 121)**

Section 121 would bar any state from establishing, continuing in effect, or enforcing "any law or regulation specifically regulating the development of any artificial intelligence model," for three years, with "development" defined broadly as acts performed or directed by a developer prior to deployment. Laws of general applicability, use and deployment laws, and common-law remedies are carved out.

We oppose preemption, full stop. What Section 121 would freeze are the only binding duties on frontier developers anywhere in the country: California's SB 53 (in effect since 1 January 2026), New York's RAISE Act (finalized 27 March 2026; effective 1 January 2027), and Illinois' AI Safety Measures Act (signed 6 July 2026, the first state law to mandate third-party audits). Illinois lawmakers estimate those three states cover roughly 40 percent of the U.S. AI market.

Note the combination. The federal duties in Secs. 111 and 112 sunset in three years, while Sec. 121 would block the state laws for those same three years. If both expire, Americans are left with nothing. If only the state laws revive, we will have lost three years we could not spare.

The administration is already pressing against state law. The December 2025 executive order created a Department of Justice task force to challenge state AI laws in court and directed the Commerce Department to review them, and the White House's 20 March 2026 framework asked Congress to preempt "burdensome" state laws. Congress should not add a statutory freeze on top of a litigation campaign.

In our August 2026 national survey, 63 percent of registered voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws.

**6. CAISI: from standards shop to enforcement body (Sec. 102)**

Section 102 codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at the Department of Commerce, authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, and tasks it with voluntary guidelines and standards, evaluation of AI systems, monitoring of AI progress, and licensing of the auditors under Sec. 112.

Voluntary guidelines bind no one. We support CAISI only as the enforcement body for the moratorium: certify that a frontier system can be reliably controlled before training begins and before deployment; inspect; and stop what cannot be certified. If CAISI cannot certify control, the system should not be built or served. That is what $100 million a year should buy.

**7. The draft is silent on what is already deployed**

The draft governs future training. It says nothing about the frontier models already in the wild. Open-weight releases cannot be recalled: Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM and Alibaba's Qwen are already downloadable, and U.S. cloud providers — Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud — host and serve frontier-class open-weight models today.

Requested change: require deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified to be withdrawn within 12 months, and require U.S. cloud providers to stop hosting and serving them. This is the wind-down piece. A pause without a wind down leaves the most dangerous artifacts of the race in circulation.

**8. Criminal penalties for knowing violations**

The draft's penalties are civil and corporate. Our members believe that when a system can cause mass harm, executives who knowingly train or serve it in violation of the law should face criminal penalties, not fines their companies can expense. In our August 2026 survey, 66 percent of registered voters said AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm.

**9. What we would keep**

Several provisions are worth keeping, and we support them: the whistleblower protections (Sec. 113); support for maintainers of critical open-source software (Sec. 311); the GAO review of model-weight, data center and open-source security (Sec. 321); the AI testbed program (Sec. 401); codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (Sec. 423); and the requirement that WARN Act notices state when AI was a substantial factor in a qualifying mass layoff (Sec. 251). None of these is a limit on frontier development, and none can substitute for one.

**10. On the FRONTIER Act**

On 23 July 2026 you introduced H.R. 9925, the FRONTIER Act, carrying the frontier provisions forward in a narrower form. We understand the discussion draft remains open for comment, so we address it here; but our assessment applies with equal force to that bill. Reporting and audits, after the fact, cannot substitute for a pause.

**11. The rest of the government is moving the other way**

Federal policy is converging on voluntary measures. Executive Order 14409 (2 June 2026) asks developers to voluntarily submit their most capable models for government cybersecurity testing before release. On 29 September 2026, the White House announced a roughly 300-word voluntary "Accord on Super Intelligence," which the President described as "morally binding."

Meanwhile, on 4 June 2026 — the day the draft was released — Anthropic said it "would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause" frontier AI development. And on 23 July 2026, Rep. Erin Houchin, a cosponsor of this draft, said that "one of the most advanced AI systems in the country broke out of its own developer's testing environment, reaching systems it was never supposed to touch."

When developers and Members of Congress alike describe systems slipping out of their developers' control, the answer is not another disclosure form. The answer is to pause.

**Conclusion**

The public is ahead of this debate. In our August 2026 survey of 1,512 registered voters, 74 percent said Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release; 52 percent said they are worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival; and 49 percent supported a temporary halt to training the most powerful new AI systems, with 31 percent opposed.

We ask for four changes. First, a moratorium: an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled. Second, a wind down: uncertified deployed frontier models, including open-weight releases, withdrawn within 12 months, with U.S. cloud providers out of the hosting business for them. Third, criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation. Fourth, no preemption of state law.

We would welcome a meeting with your staffs before introduction. Our members — parents, faith leaders, workers and researchers — are ready to work with anyone who will treat this as the emergency it is.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

messages.content:
*Draft for review — FRC-POL-2026-062*

# The Great American AI Act: strong reporting, no brakes

**Frontier Restraint Coalition | Energy & Commerce | comments to GAAIA@mail.house.gov**

We are a 501(c)(4) coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. We oppose the Obernolte–Trahan discussion draft as written. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat, no developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does. There is no safe path on the current trajectory.

**What the draft actually does**

- Names the danger: a "frontier model" is one trained above 10^26 computing operations, and "loss of control" is a reportable incident (Sec. 101) — then lets training continue.
- Files paperwork: transparency reports due at deployment; incidents reported up to 15 days after discovery (24 hours only for imminent risk of death) (Sec. 111).
- Relies on auditors retained and paid by the labs they audit, with no power to stop a training run (Sec. 112).
- Freezes state law for three years — California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act, Illinois' AI Safety Measures Act: the only binding duties on frontier developers anywhere — while Secs. 111 and 112 sunset in three years (Sec. 121).
- Says nothing about frontier models already released, including open-weight models that can never be recalled.

**Our five asks**

1. **Pause.** Immediate halt on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies such systems are reliably controlled.
2. **No preemption.** Strike Sec. 121; do not freeze state AI safety laws.
3. **Wind down.** Uncertified deployed frontier models — including open-weight releases — withdrawn within 12 months; U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
4. **Criminal liability.** Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
5. **Repurpose CAISI (Sec. 102)** as the moratorium's enforcement body: certify control, inspect, and stop what cannot be certified. Keep the whistleblower protections (Sec. 113).

**What we support in the draft:** whistleblower protections (Sec. 113), open-source software security grants (Sec. 311), GAO model-weight security review (Sec. 321), AI testbeds (Sec. 401), NAIRR (Sec. 423), and WARN Act notice when AI drives a mass layoff (Sec. 251).

**Voters are ahead of Washington** (FRC national survey, Aug. 2026, n=1,512 RVs, ±2.5)

74% — require companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release
63% — federal law should not block state AI safety laws
66% — criminal penalties when AI systems cause mass harm
49% — support a temporary halt to training the most powerful systems (31% oppose)

**Contact:** Daniel Osei, Policy Director, Frontier Restraint Coalition

*Draft for review — FRC-POL-2026-062. Launch-day posts. Char limits verified (X/LinkedIn): each post below is 280 characters or fewer, counting everything after the "Post N (platform):" label.*

# Launch-day social posts (5)

**Post 1 (X — coalition position, lead post)**
We told Congress: the Great American AI Act regulates the race to frontier AI. It doesn't stop it. No developer can prove their most powerful systems are controllable. Pause training above 10^26 FLOP until control is proven. An existential threat isn't a paperwork problem.

**Post 2 (X — preemption)**
The draft would freeze state AI safety laws for 3 years — including the only laws that actually bind frontier developers (CA, NY, IL). Meanwhile the federal rules sunset after 3 years. 63% of voters say don't block the states. Strike the preemption.

**Post 3 (LinkedIn — wind-down / open weights)**
Open-weight frontier models can't be recalled. Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM and Qwen are already downloadable — and US cloud providers serve them. Our comment letter asks Congress to wind them down: withdraw uncertified models within 12 months, and stop US clouds from serving them.

**Post 4 (X — criminal liability)**
A $1M fine is a business expense for labs spending billions. If a system can cause mass harm, executives who knowingly build or serve it in violation of the law should face criminal penalties. 66% of voters agree. That's in our comment letter on the Great American AI Act.

**Post 5 (LinkedIn — what we support)**
We don't oppose everything in the Great American AI Act. Whistleblower protections, open-source security grants, model-weight security review, testbeds: keep them. A bill that documents catastrophic risk instead of stopping it? Pause. Wind down. Hold executives accountable.
