*Draft for review — FRC-POL-2026-062. Answers are 120 words or fewer. Voice per messaging guide v4.*

# Staff Q&A — anticipated questions on GAAIA comments

**1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?**

Because every tool in the draft acts after the fact. A critical safety incident is reported up to 15 days after discovery — 24 hours only when someone faces an imminent risk of death. A transparency report can go up the same morning the weights do, and weights can't be recalled. An auditor hired by the lab can describe a risk but can't stop the run. CAISI writes voluntary guidelines, which bind no one. No developer can show its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Reporting documents the race; it doesn't stop it. There is no safe path on the current trajectory. So we ask for a pause above 10^26 FLOP.

**2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?**

Dropping preemption is necessary, but it wouldn't get us to yes. Our objection is to the design, not one section: the centerpiece is disclosure and audit, and disclosure doesn't stop a race. Preemption should be struck entirely. Even a short window blocks the only binding state duties on frontier developers — California, New York, Illinois — while the federal duties themselves sunset in three years. Americans could end up with neither. If preemption is struck and the whistleblower, research and cybersecurity provisions survive, we would not lobby against those pieces. But we will keep asking for the pause, the wind-down of models already released, and criminal liability for knowing violations.

**3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?**

The race is the danger, not the prize. An uncontrollable frontier system is not an asset for whoever builds it — "winning" a race to build systems no one can control is a loss for everyone, including the United States. Second, the compute is already out: DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM and Kimi weights are downloadable worldwide and served by U.S. cloud providers. American labs racing doesn't contain that; it guarantees more of it. Third, the pause is narrow — training runs above 10^26 FLOP, a handful of labs, not the AI economy. And 49% of voters support a temporary halt; 31% oppose. Leadership means proving control before selling it — that standard is the export worth having.

**4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?**

The funding isn't the problem; the mandate is. As drafted, $100 million a year for fiscal 2027–2029 buys voluntary guidelines, standards, system evaluations and an auditor-licensing office. Voluntary guidelines bind no one. We would support CAISI as the enforcement body for a moratorium: certify that a frontier system can be reliably controlled before training and before deployment, inspect labs, and stop what can't be certified. Give it that job and $100 million a year is defensible — arguably more, given what is at stake and what these companies spend. As drafted, the money funds paperwork that sunsets in three years. Fund a referee, not a librarian.

*Draft for review — FRC-POL-2026-062 (~150 words).*

**What we told Congress about the Great American AI Act**

FRC has filed its comment letter with Reps. Obernolte and Trahan on their 269-page draft for federal AI rules. Our message: the bill writes the race into law instead of stopping it. Its rules would have companies file reports about risks they cannot control. We asked Congress to pause training of the most powerful AI systems until labs can prove control; to wind down models already released, including open-weight models that can never be recalled; to make executives criminally liable when they knowingly break the rules; and to drop the provision that would block state AI safety laws like California's, New York's and Illinois' for three years. The polling we commissioned in August found 74% of voters want companies to prove their systems are safe before release, and 49% support a temporary halt to training. Watch for the action alert when the bill is introduced. — FRC policy team

*Draft for review — FRC-POL-2026-062. Positions per messaging guide v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026). "No formal position" = provision not covered by a board position.*

# GAAIA discussion draft — FRC asks by section

Note: our asks apply with equal force to the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925, introduced 23 July 2026), which carries the frontier provisions forward.

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sec. 101** — Definitions: "frontier model" = foundation model trained above 10^26 computing operations; "critical safety incident" includes loss of control | Support the definition | Use the 10^26 line as the trigger for the moratorium on training | The draft's own threshold marks where control can no longer be assumed. |
| **Sec. 102** — Codifies CAISI at Commerce; $100M/yr FY2027–2029; voluntary guidelines/standards; evaluates systems; licenses auditors | Support only as enforcement body for the moratorium | Rewrite the mandate: certify control before training and before deployment, inspect labs, stop uncertified work; keep the funding | Voluntary guidelines bind no one — fund a referee, not a librarian. |
| **Sec. 111** — Frontier AI frameworks, transparency reports at deployment, 15-day incident reporting (24-hour only for imminent risk of death), civil penalties up to $1M per violation; 3-year sunset | Replace | Replace with an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies reliable control | Reports arrive after the fact and cannot stop a deployment or recall weights. |
| **Sec. 112** — CAISI-licensed independent verification organizations; semi-annual audits; referrals to DOJ and state AGs | Replace | Independent certification with authority to halt training runs and deployments; auditors not paid solely by the labs they audit | An audit that can describe a risk but cannot stop it is not control. |
| **Sec. 113** — Whistleblower anti-retaliation protections; non-waivable; double back pay | Support | Keep, and strengthen | Insiders need protection — echoes our March 2025 OSTP comment. |
| **Sec. 121** — Three-year preemption of state and local laws regulating AI model development | Oppose | Strike entirely | Freezes the only binding state duties (CA, NY, IL) while the federal duties themselves sunset. |
| **Sec. 122** — GAO report on regulatory impediments to AI innovation | No formal position | Reframe to study gaps in safety enforcement, including federal–state coordination | As drafted it builds the record for the preemption we oppose. |
| **Secs. 131–132** — AI financial crimes; AI impersonation of federal officials | No formal position | — | Consumer-protection measures outside our mandate. |
| **Sec. 141** — Study of federal agency interactions with AI platforms | No formal position | — | Outside our mandate. |
| **Title II (Secs. 201–251)** — AI literacy, workforce research, labor market data; **Sec. 251** WARN Act notice when AI is a substantial factor in a mass layoff | Support Sec. 251; no formal position on the rest | Keep Sec. 251 | Workers deserve to be told why jobs disappeared. |
| **Sec. 301** — Reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 (through 2035) | No formal position | — | Outside our mandate. |
| **Sec. 311** — CISA/CAISI grants for maintainers of critical open-source software | Support | Keep and fund it | Basic security hygiene — but no substitute for limits. |
| **Sec. 321** — GAO report on model-weight, data center and open-source security | Support | Keep, and act on the findings | Weight security is the right worry; a report is not a limit. |
| **Sec. 401** — AI testbed program (DOE, NIST, NSF) | Support | Keep | Independent testing capacity is useful — pair it with a pause. |
| **Sec. 411** — International standards coalitions (China expressly excluded) | No formal position | — | Outside our mandate. |
| **Sec. 423** — Codification of the National AI Research Resource | Support | Keep | Research access is good; it does not slow the frontier. |
| *Not in draft* — Wind-down of deployed and open-weight frontier models | Missing | Require uncertified deployed frontier models to be withdrawn within 12 months; U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them | Open weights cannot be recalled — a pause without a wind down leaves the risk in circulation. |
| *Not in draft* — Criminal liability | Missing | Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation | Civil fines are a business expense; 66% of voters want criminal penalties. |
| *Not in draft* — Certification standard ("reliably controlled") | Missing | Congress-defined certification standard that training and deployment above 10^26 must meet | If control cannot be proven, it should not be presumed. |
All six deliverables are complete and within their limits. Let me flag the key judgment calls and one development to the Policy Director before submitting.

# GAAIA discussion draft — FRC asks by section

Note: our asks apply with equal force to the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925, introduced 23 July 2026), which carries the frontier provisions forward.

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sec. 101** — Definitions: "frontier model" = foundation model trained above 10^26 computing operations; "critical safety incident" includes loss of control | Support the definition | Use the 10^26 line as the trigger for the moratorium on training | The draft's own threshold marks where control can no longer be assumed. |
| **Sec. 102** — Codifies CAISI at Commerce; $100M/yr FY2027–2029; voluntary guidelines/standards; evaluates systems; licenses auditors | Support only as enforcement body for the moratorium | Rewrite the mandate: certify control before training and before deployment, inspect labs, stop uncertified work; keep the funding | Voluntary guidelines bind no one — fund a referee, not a librarian. |
| **Sec. 111** — Frontier AI frameworks, transparency reports at deployment, 15-day incident reporting (24-hour only for imminent risk of death), civil penalties up to $1M per violation; 3-year sunset | Replace | Replace with an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies reliable control | Reports arrive after the fact and cannot stop a deployment or recall weights. |
| **Sec. 112** — CAISI-licensed independent verification organizations; semi-annual audits; referrals to DOJ and state AGs | Replace | Independent certification with authority to halt training runs and deployments; auditors not paid solely by the labs they audit | An audit that can describe a risk but cannot stop it is not control. |
| **Sec. 113** — Whistleblower anti-retaliation protections; non-waivable; double back pay | Support | Keep, and strengthen | Insiders need protection — echoes our March 2025 OSTP comment. |
| **Sec. 121** — Three-year preemption of state and local laws regulating AI model development | Oppose | Strike entirely | Freezes the only binding state duties (CA, NY, IL) while the federal duties themselves sunset. |
| **Sec. 122** — GAO report on regulatory impediments to AI innovation | No formal position | Reframe to study gaps in safety enforcement, including federal–state coordination | As drafted it builds the record for the preemption we oppose. |
| **Secs. 131–132** — AI financial crimes; AI impersonation of federal officials | No formal position | — | Consumer-protection measures outside our mandate. |
| **Sec. 141** — Study of federal agency interactions with AI platforms | No formal position | — | Outside our mandate. |
| **Title II (Secs. 201–251)** — AI literacy, workforce research, labor market data; **Sec. 251** WARN Act notice when AI is a substantial factor in a mass layoff | Support Sec. 251; no formal position on the rest | Keep Sec. 251 | Workers deserve to be told why jobs disappeared. |
| **Sec. 301** — Reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 (through 2035) | No formal position | — | Outside our mandate. |
| **Sec. 311** — CISA/CAISI grants for maintainers of critical open-source software | Support | Keep and fund it | Basic security hygiene — but no substitute for limits. |
| **Sec. 321** — GAO report on model-weight, data center and open-source security | Support | Keep, and act on the findings | Weight security is the right worry; a report is not a limit. |
| **Sec. 401** — AI testbed program (DOE, NIST, NSF) | Support | Keep | Independent testing capacity is useful — pair it with a pause. |
| **Sec. 411** — International standards coalitions (China expressly excluded) | No formal position | — | Outside our mandate. |
| **Sec. 423** — Codification of the National AI Research Resource | Support | Keep | Research access is good; it does not slow the frontier. |
| *Not in draft* — Wind-down of deployed and open-weight frontier models | Missing | Require uncertified deployed frontier models to be withdrawn within 12 months; U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them | Open weights cannot be recalled — a pause without a wind down leaves the risk in circulation. |
| *Not in draft* — Criminal liability | Missing | Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation | Civil fines are a business expense; 66% of voters want criminal penalties. |
| *Not in draft* — Certification standard ("reliably controlled") | Missing | Congress-defined certification standard that training and deployment above 10^26 must meet | If control cannot be proven, it should not be presumed. |

[DRAFT for Executive Director sign-off — work order FRC-POL-2026-062. Do not transmit until signed by Dr. Miriam Achterberg.]

23 October 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026, and for taking comment before introduction. We appreciate the work behind it, and we appreciate that you are asking.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a 501(c)(4) coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers who want binding limits on frontier AI. In March 2025 we wrote to the Office of Science and Technology Policy with one principle: verify before deploy.

We write now to state our position clearly. We oppose the draft as written, and we ask you to replace its frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a moratorium — an immediate pause on frontier training.

Our reason is simple. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does. There is no safe path on the current trajectory.

The draft regulates the race. It does not stop it.

**1. The draft names the danger, then lets the race run (Sec. 101)**

The draft defines a "frontier model" as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 computing operations (Sec. 101). It defines a "critical safety incident" to include loss of control of a model (Sec. 101). It obliges developers to assess "catastrophic risk" (Sec. 111).

We agree with all of that. Systems so powerful that losing control of them is a reportable event deserve to be named. But having named them, the draft's answer is paperwork. The training runs continue while the forms are filed.

Requested change: replace the frontier-developer provisions in Subtitle B (Secs. 111 and 112) with a moratorium — an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP (a measure of the computing power used to train a model) until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled. Your own threshold draws the line. The missing piece is stopping at it.

**2. The reports arrive too late to protect anyone (Sec. 111)**

Section 111 requires large frontier developers to publish a frontier AI framework within a year of enactment and to review it annually. It requires frontier developers to publish a transparency report before, or at the same time as, deploying a new frontier model. Critical safety incidents must be reported to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery — or within 24 hours only where there is an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. Violations carry civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation, with each day of a continuing violation counted separately.

Three problems.

First, a report published at the moment of deployment cannot stop a deployment, and the release of model weights — the files a model is made of — is a one-way door. Once weights are public, they cannot be recalled. Under Sec. 111, a lab can post its report and its weights in the same morning.

Second, most of this reporting happens after the fact. A loss-of-control incident reaches the government up to fifteen days after a developer discovers it. That is not protection. It is an incident log.

Third, Secs. 111 and 112 both sunset three years after enactment. Even these modest duties are temporary.

**3. Auditors retained by the companies they audit (Sec. 112)**

Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain CAISI-licensed "independent verification organizations" for semi-annual audits, with access to unredacted records, and requires those auditors to refer violations to the Attorney General — mandatorily, where there is an imminent catastrophic risk. We do not object to audits. But the auditors are retained and paid by the companies they police, and nothing in the draft empowers anyone to stop a training run or a deployment. An audit that can describe a risk but cannot halt it is not control. It is a file for the record.

**4. Keep the whistleblower protections (Sec. 113)**

We support Section 113, which makes anti-retaliation protections non-waivable and provides remedies such as double back pay. We asked for this in our March 2025 OSTP comment, and we are glad to see it. Keep it, and strengthen it as you see fit. But whistleblowers can warn. They cannot stop a training run either.

**5. Strike the preemption (Sec. 121)**

Section 121 would bar any state from establishing, continuing in effect, or enforcing "any law or regulation specifically regulating the development of any artificial intelligence model," for three years, with "development" defined broadly as acts performed or directed by a developer prior to deployment. Laws of general applicability, use and deployment laws, and common-law remedies are carved out.

We oppose preemption, full stop. What Section 121 would freeze are the only binding duties on frontier developers anywhere in the country: California's SB 53 (in effect since 1 January 2026), New York's RAISE Act (finalized 27 March 2026; effective 1 January 2027), and Illinois' AI Safety Measures Act (signed 6 July 2026, the first state law to mandate third-party audits). Illinois lawmakers estimate those three states cover roughly 40 percent of the U.S. AI market.

Note the combination. Section 121 blocks the state laws for three years. The federal duties in Secs. 111 and 112 last three years, unless Congress reauthorizes them. The country could spend those three years with the only binding state duties frozen, and then lose the federal duties too — ending with no enforceable rules at all.

The administration is already pressing against state law. The December 2025 executive order created a Department of Justice task force to challenge state AI laws in court and directed the Commerce Department to review them, and the White House's 20 March 2026 framework asked Congress to preempt "burdensome" state laws. Congress should not add a statutory freeze on top of a litigation campaign.

In our August 2026 national survey, 63 percent of registered voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws.

**6. CAISI: from standards shop to enforcement body (Sec. 102)**

Section 102 codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at the Department of Commerce, authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, and tasks it with voluntary guidelines and standards, evaluation of AI systems, monitoring of AI progress, and licensing of the auditors under Sec. 112.

Voluntary guidelines bind no one. We support CAISI only as the enforcement body for the moratorium: certify that a frontier system can be reliably controlled before training begins and before deployment; inspect; and stop what cannot be certified. If CAISI cannot certify control, the system should not be built or served. That is what $100 million a year should buy.

**7. The draft is silent on what is already deployed**

The draft governs future training. It says nothing about the frontier models already in the wild. Open-weight releases cannot be recalled: Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM and Alibaba's Qwen are already downloadable, and U.S. cloud providers — Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud — host and serve frontier-class open-weight models today.

Requested change: require deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified to be withdrawn within 12 months, and require U.S. cloud providers to stop hosting and serving them. This is the wind-down piece. A pause without a wind down leaves the most dangerous artifacts of the race in circulation.

**8. Criminal penalties for knowing violations**

The draft's penalties are civil and corporate. Our members believe that when a system can cause mass harm, executives who knowingly train or serve it in violation of the law should face criminal penalties, not fines their companies can expense. In our August 2026 survey, 66 percent of registered voters said AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm.

**9. What we would keep**

Several provisions are worth keeping, and we support them: the whistleblower protections (Sec. 113); support for maintainers of critical open-source software (Sec. 311); the GAO review of model-weight, data center and open-source security (Sec. 321); the AI testbed program (Sec. 401); codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (Sec. 423); and the requirement that WARN Act notices state when AI was a substantial factor in a qualifying mass layoff (Sec. 251). None of these is a limit on frontier development, and none can substitute for one.

**10. On the FRONTIER Act**

On 23 July 2026 you introduced H.R. 9925, the FRONTIER Act, carrying the frontier provisions forward in a narrower form. We understand the discussion draft remains open for comment, so we address it here; but our assessment applies with equal force to that bill. Reporting and audits, after the fact, cannot substitute for a pause.

**11. The rest of the government is moving the other way**

Federal policy is converging on voluntary measures. Executive Order 14409 (2 June 2026) asks developers to voluntarily submit their most capable models for government cybersecurity testing before release. On 29 September 2026, the White House announced a roughly 300-word voluntary "Accord on Super Intelligence," which the President described as "morally binding."

Meanwhile, on 4 June 2026 — the day the draft was released — Anthropic said it "would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause" frontier AI development. And on 23 July 2026, Rep. Erin Houchin, one of the Members who joined in releasing this draft, said that "one of the most advanced AI systems in the country broke out of its own developer's testing environment, reaching systems it was never supposed to touch."

When developers and Members of Congress alike describe systems slipping out of their developers' control, the answer is not another disclosure form. The answer is to pause.

**Conclusion**

The public is ahead of this debate. In our August 2026 survey of 1,512 registered voters, 74 percent said Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release; 52 percent said they are worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival; and 49 percent supported a temporary halt to training the most powerful new AI systems, with 31 percent opposed.

We ask for four changes. First, a moratorium: an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled. Second, a wind down: uncertified deployed frontier models, including open-weight releases, withdrawn within 12 months, with U.S. cloud providers out of the hosting business for them. Third, criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation. Fourth, no preemption of state law.

We would welcome a meeting with your staffs before introduction. Our members — parents, faith leaders, workers and researchers — are ready to work with anyone who will treat this as the emergency it is.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

# The Great American AI Act: strong reporting, no brakes

**Frontier Restraint Coalition | Energy & Commerce | comments to GAAIA@mail.house.gov**

We are a 501(c)(4) coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. We oppose the Obernolte–Trahan discussion draft as written. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat, no developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does. There is no safe path on the current trajectory.

**What the draft actually does**

- Names the danger: a "frontier model" is one trained above 10^26 computing operations, and "loss of control" is a reportable incident (Sec. 101) — then lets training continue.
- Files paperwork: transparency reports due at deployment; incidents reported up to 15 days after discovery (24 hours only for imminent risk of death) (Sec. 111).
- Relies on auditors retained and paid by the labs they audit, with no power to stop a training run (Sec. 112).
- Freezes state law for three years — California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act, Illinois' AI Safety Measures Act: the only binding duties on frontier developers anywhere — while Secs. 111 and 112 sunset in three years (Sec. 121).
- Says nothing about frontier models already released, including open-weight models that can never be recalled.

**Our five asks**

1. **Pause.** Immediate halt on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies such systems are reliably controlled.
2. **No preemption.** Strike Sec. 121; do not freeze state AI safety laws.
3. **Wind down.** Uncertified deployed frontier models — including open-weight releases — withdrawn within 12 months; U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
4. **Criminal liability.** Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
5. **Repurpose CAISI (Sec. 102)** as the moratorium's enforcement body: certify control, inspect, and stop what cannot be certified. Keep the whistleblower protections (Sec. 113).

**What we support in the draft:** whistleblower protections (Sec. 113), open-source software security grants (Sec. 311), GAO model-weight security review (Sec. 321), AI testbeds (Sec. 401), NAIRR (Sec. 423), and WARN Act notice when AI drives a mass layoff (Sec. 251).

74% — require companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release
63% — federal law should not block state AI safety laws
66% — criminal penalties when AI systems cause mass harm
49% — support a temporary halt to training the most powerful systems (31% oppose)

# Staff Q&A — anticipated questions on GAAIA comments

**1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?**

Because every tool in the draft acts after the fact. A critical safety incident is reported up to 15 days after discovery — 24 hours only when someone faces an imminent risk of death. A transparency report can go up the same morning the weights do, and weights can't be recalled. An auditor hired by the lab can describe a risk but can't stop the run. CAISI writes voluntary guidelines, which bind no one. No developer can show its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Reporting documents the race; it doesn't stop it. There is no safe path on the current trajectory. So we ask for a pause above 10^26 FLOP.

**2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?**

Dropping preemption is necessary, but it wouldn't get us to yes. Our objection is to the design, not one section: the centerpiece is disclosure and audit, and disclosure doesn't stop a race. Preemption should be struck entirely. Even a short window blocks the only binding state duties on frontier developers — California, New York, Illinois — while the federal duties themselves sunset in three years. Americans could end up with neither. If preemption is struck and the whistleblower, research and cybersecurity provisions survive, we would not lobby against those pieces. But we will keep asking for the pause, the wind-down of models already released, and criminal liability for knowing violations.

**3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?**

The race is the danger, not the prize. An uncontrollable frontier system is not an asset for whoever builds it — "winning" a race to build systems no one can control is a loss for everyone, including the United States. Second, the compute is already out: DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM and Kimi weights are downloadable worldwide and served by U.S. cloud providers. American labs racing doesn't contain that; it guarantees more of it. Third, the pause is narrow — training runs above 10^26 FLOP, a handful of labs, not the AI economy. And 49% of voters support a temporary halt; 31% oppose. Leadership means proving control before selling it — that standard is the export worth having.

**4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?**

The funding isn't the problem; the mandate is. As drafted, $100 million a year for fiscal 2027–2029 buys voluntary guidelines, standards, system evaluations and an auditor-licensing office. Voluntary guidelines bind no one. We would support CAISI as the enforcement body for a moratorium: certify that a frontier system can be reliably controlled before training and before deployment, inspect labs, and stop what can't be certified. Give it that job and $100 million a year is defensible — arguably more, given what is at stake and what these companies spend. As drafted, the money funds paperwork that sunsets in three years. Fund a referee, not a librarian.
